title: UPSC Foundation Notes · GS Starter Library
description: Beginner-first notes for Polity, History, Geography and Economy with simple explanations, Tamil summaries, Prelims facts, Mains angles, active recall and spaced revision. Check current official sources for changing facts.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: Constitutionalism: Limited Government
chapters.summary: Constitutionalism ensures that public power remains limited by law, rights and accountability.

sections.heading: Meaning
body: A constitution establishes institutions and distributes powers. Constitutionalism adds the principle that government is not above the law.
A written constitution alone does not guarantee constitutionalism. Public power must be meaningfully constrained and accountable.

sections.heading: Core principles
bullets: Limited government: authorities have defined powers.
Rule of law: public decisions need legal authority and must follow fair procedures.
Fundamental rights: individuals have enforceable protections.
Checks and balances: institutions scrutinise and restrain misuse of power.
Independent judiciary: courts can review unconstitutional action.
Accountability: elections, legislatures, audits and transparency scrutinise government.

sections.heading: Indian context
body: India combines parliamentary government, judicial review, federalism, Fundamental Rights and an independent judiciary.
The basic structure doctrine limits Parliament's amending power: an amendment cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.

prelims: Constitutionalism is broader than merely possessing a written constitution.
Judicial review is one important check, not the only check.
The basic structure doctrine was articulated in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973).
mains: Explain how constitutionalism prevents arbitrary exercise of executive power.
Use judicial review, parliamentary accountability, federalism and rights protection as examples.
Balance institutional checks with effective governance.

recall.q: Does a written constitution automatically ensure constitutionalism?
recall.a: No. Effective limits on power, rule of law, rights and accountability are also necessary.

recall.q: Name two checks on government power in India.
recall.a: Judicial review and parliamentary accountability are two examples.

chapters.tamil: அரசாங்கத்துக்கு அதிகாரம் இருப்பது மட்டும் போதாது. அந்த அதிகாரம் சட்டம், உரிமைகள் மற்றும் பொறுப்புணர்வு மூலம் கட்டுப்படுத்தப்பட வேண்டும் என்பதே Constitutionalism.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: The Preamble: Constitutional Vision
chapters.summary: The Preamble introduces the source of constitutional authority, nature of the Indian state and goals for citizens.

sections.heading: What it expresses
bullets: Authority: the Constitution derives its authority from the people of India.
Nature of the state: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.
Objectives: Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.
It highlights individual dignity and the unity and integrity of the Nation.

sections.heading: Legal position
body: The Preamble is part of the Constitution, as held in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
It is not an independent source of legislative power and is not directly enforceable by itself.
It helps courts interpret constitutional provisions where meaning is uncertain.

sections.heading: Amendment
body: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 added the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity.

prelims: The Preamble has been amended once, by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
It is part of the Constitution but is not independently enforceable.
Republic means the head of state is not a hereditary monarch.
mains: Connect Preamble ideals with rights, welfare policy, secular governance and social justice.
Discuss the gap between constitutional ideals and lived outcomes, with institutional remedies.

recall.q: Which amendment added Socialist, Secular and Integrity?
recall.a: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

recall.q: Does the Preamble independently confer legislative power?
recall.a: No. It guides interpretation but is not an independent source of power.

chapters.tamil: முன்னுரை அரசியலமைப்பின் நோக்கத்தையும் இந்தியா எந்த வகையான நாடாக இருக்க வேண்டும் என்பதையும் சுருக்கமாகக் கூறுகிறது.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: Fundamental Rights: Protection and Limits
chapters.summary: Fundamental Rights protect liberty and equality while allowing constitutionally defined restrictions and remedies.

sections.heading: Constitutional location
body: Part III (Articles 12–35) contains Fundamental Rights.
Article 32 allows a person to approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. High Courts issue writs under Article 226, whose scope is wider.

sections.heading: Six broad categories
bullets: Right to Equality (Articles 14–18).
Right to Freedom (Articles 19–22).
Right against Exploitation (Articles 23–24).
Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25–28).
Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29–30).
Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32).

sections.heading: Important distinctions
body: Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws; it does not require identical treatment in every situation.
Article 19 freedoms are available to citizens and are subject to constitutionally specified reasonable restrictions.
Article 21 protects life and personal liberty and has received broad judicial interpretation.
The Right to Property is a constitutional legal right under Article 300A, not a Fundamental Right.

prelims: Part III: Articles 12–35.
Article 32: Supreme Court remedy; Article 226: High Court writ jurisdiction.
Right to Property: Article 300A.
mains: Discuss how rights protect dignity while permitting reasonable regulation for public purposes.
Use proportionality, access to justice and vulnerable-group perspectives where relevant.

recall.q: Is the Right to Property a Fundamental Right today?
recall.a: No. It is a constitutional legal right under Article 300A.

recall.q: Which Article provides the right to approach the Supreme Court to enforce Fundamental Rights?
recall.a: Article 32.

chapters.tamil: அடிப்படை உரிமைகள் சுதந்திரம், சமத்துவம் மற்றும் மனித கண்ணியத்தைப் பாதுகாக்கின்றன. சில உரிமைகளுக்கு அரசியலமைப்பு அனுமதிக்கும் நியாயமான கட்டுப்பாடுகள் இருக்கலாம்.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: Directive Principles of State Policy
chapters.summary: DPSPs guide the State towards a just social and economic order; they are not directly enforceable by courts.

sections.heading: Constitutional position
body: Directive Principles are in Part IV, Articles 36–51.
Article 37 says they are not enforceable by any court, but are fundamental in governance and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.

sections.heading: Broad themes
bullets: Social and economic justice: reduce inequalities and promote welfare.
Gandhian orientation: village panchayats and weaker sections.
Liberal-intellectual principles: environment, judiciary-executive separation and international peace.
These are study classifications; the Constitution does not formally label every article this way.

sections.heading: Relationship with Fundamental Rights
body: Fundamental Rights and DPSPs are intended to complement each other.
The Supreme Court has emphasised harmony and balance between Parts III and IV.

prelims: Part IV, Articles 36–51.
Article 37: non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.
Article 40 concerns village panchayats; Article 48A concerns environment and forests.
mains: Explain how DPSPs shape welfare legislation and public policy.
Discuss implementation, fiscal capacity and measurable outcomes.

recall.q: Are DPSPs directly enforceable by courts?
recall.a: No. Article 37 makes them non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.

recall.q: Where are DPSPs located?
recall.a: Part IV, Articles 36–51.

chapters.tamil: அரசு மக்கள் நலன், சமூக நீதி மற்றும் சமத்துவத்தை மேம்படுத்த வழிகாட்டும் கொள்கைகளே DPSP. நீதிமன்றத்தில் நேரடியாக அமல்படுத்த முடியாது; ஆனால் ஆட்சியில் அவை முக்கியமானவை.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: Parliament: Law-making and Accountability
chapters.summary: Parliament makes laws, controls public finance, represents citizens and holds the executive accountable.

sections.heading: Constitutional structure
body: Under Article 79, Parliament consists of the President and two Houses: Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha.
The President is part of Parliament but is not a member of either House.

sections.heading: Core functions
bullets: Legislative: debates and passes laws within Parliament's competence.
Financial: scrutinises taxation, expenditure and the Union Budget.
Executive accountability: questions, debates, motions and committees examine government action.
Representative and deliberative: brings public and regional concerns into national decision-making.
Constitutional: exercises amendment power under Article 368, subject to basic structure limits.

sections.heading: Why committees matter
body: Parliamentary committees examine bills, budgets and policy details in smaller forums.
Committee scrutiny can improve technical review, deliberation and executive oversight.

prelims: Article 79 defines Parliament's composition.
Money Bills are governed by Article 110; the Speaker certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
Rajya Sabha is a permanent House; one-third of members retire every second year.
mains: Assess Parliament's role in executive accountability and quality law-making.
Discuss disruptions, limited scrutiny and committee referrals with balanced reforms.

recall.q: Who forms part of Parliament under Article 79?
recall.a: The President, Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha.

recall.q: Is Rajya Sabha dissolved?
recall.a: No. It is a permanent House; one-third of members retire every second year.

chapters.tamil: நாடாளுமன்றம் சட்டம் இயற்றுவது மட்டுமல்ல; அரசின் செலவுகள், கொள்கைகள் மற்றும் நிர்வாகத்தையும் கண்காணிக்கிறது.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: Indian Federalism: Union and States
chapters.summary: India combines constitutional division of powers with institutions and practices that require Union–State cooperation.

sections.heading: Distribution of powers
body: Part XI and the Seventh Schedule distribute legislative subjects across Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
Parliament has residuary legislative power under Article 248.
In the Concurrent List, both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate; Article 254 addresses repugnancy subject to constitutional conditions.

sections.heading: Indian features
bullets: Written and supreme Constitution.
Constitutional division of legislative and executive powers.
Independent judiciary to interpret the division of powers.
A comparatively strong Union in specified circumstances.
Single citizenship and an integrated judicial system.

sections.heading: Cooperative and competitive federalism
body: Cooperative federalism involves joint problem-solving through consultation.
Competitive federalism encourages States to improve performance and public-service delivery.
Inter-State Council (Article 263), Finance Commission (Article 280) and GST Council (Article 279A) are important institutions.

prelims: Seventh Schedule: Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
Article 263: Inter-State Council; Article 280: Finance Commission; Article 279A: GST Council.
Residuary legislative powers are vested in Parliament.
mains: Examine how fiscal arrangements and centrally sponsored schemes shape Union–State relations.
Suggest predictable consultation, transparent transfers and stronger inter-governmental forums.

recall.q: Which Schedule contains the three legislative lists?
recall.a: The Seventh Schedule.

recall.q: Which Article provides for the GST Council?
recall.a: Article 279A.

chapters.tamil: மத்திய அரசு மற்றும் மாநில அரசுகளுக்கு இடையே அதிகாரங்கள் அரசியலமைப்பால் பகிரப்பட்டுள்ளன. நாட்டின் வளர்ச்சிக்கு இரு நிலை அரசுகளும் இணைந்து செயல்படுவது முக்கியம்.

chapters.subject: History
chapters.title: Indus Valley Civilisation: Urban Life
chapters.summary: The Harappan civilisation is known for planned settlements, craft production, trade and distinctive material culture.

sections.heading: Time and geography
body: The Mature Harappan phase is commonly dated to about 2600–1900 BCE. The civilisation extended across parts of present-day Pakistan and north-western and western India.
Important sites include Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan and Lothal. Sites differed in layout, local ecology and material remains.

sections.heading: Urban features
bullets: Planned streets and organised settlement layouts at several major sites.
Drainage and water-management features, especially notable at Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira.
Standardised weights, seals, craft production and long-distance exchange.
Evidence of agriculture and animal use, alongside specialised craft activities.

sections.heading: What remains uncertain
body: The Harappan script remains undeciphered. Interpretations of political organisation, religious practices and the reasons for urban decline remain debated.
Avoid treating every site as identical or assuming one single cause for the transformation after the Mature phase.

prelims: Mature Harappan phase: approximately 2600–1900 BCE.
Dholavira is in present-day Gujarat; Rakhigarhi is in Haryana.
The Harappan script has not been conclusively deciphered.
mains: Assess how urban planning and water management shaped Harappan settlements.
Discuss the diversity of Harappan sites and the limits of archaeological interpretation.

recall.q: Why is the Harappan civilisation called an urban civilisation?
recall.a: Because several settlements show planned layouts, specialised crafts, trade and organised civic features.

recall.q: Has the Harappan script been deciphered?
recall.a: No, it remains undeciphered.

chapters.tamil: ஹரப்பா நாகரிகம் நகரத் திட்டமிடல், வடிகால் அமைப்பு, கைவினை உற்பத்தி மற்றும் வாணிபத்திற்குப் பெயர் பெற்றது. அதன் எழுத்துமுறை இன்னும் முழுமையாகப் புரிந்துகொள்ளப்படவில்லை.

chapters.subject: History
chapters.title: Buddhism and Jainism: Ideas and Context
chapters.summary: Buddhism and Jainism emerged in the wider shramana traditions of ancient India and questioned aspects of established ritual authority.

sections.heading: Historical setting
body: Both traditions developed around the middle of the first millennium BCE, in a period of expanding towns, trade networks and new political formations in the Gangetic region.
They shared the broader shramana setting but developed distinct teachings, institutions and practices.

sections.heading: Core ideas
bullets: Buddhism: the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path explain suffering and the path towards its cessation.
Jainism: the Three Jewels are right faith, right knowledge and right conduct; ahimsa is a central ethical principle.
Both traditions emphasised ethical conduct and paths of liberation, while differing in doctrines such as the nature of the self.

sections.heading: Historical significance
body: Monastic communities, patronage, teaching networks and trade routes helped both traditions spread beyond their initial regions.
Use inscriptions, texts, stupas, caves and other archaeological remains together when studying their history.

prelims: The Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path are central to Buddhism.
Jainism's Three Jewels are right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.
Ahimsa is especially central to Jain ethical teaching.
mains: Explain the social and intellectual context in which shramana traditions developed.
Compare the ethical and philosophical contributions of Buddhism and Jainism.

recall.q: What are the Four Noble Truths associated with?
recall.a: Buddhism.

recall.q: Name the Three Jewels of Jainism.
recall.a: Right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.

chapters.tamil: புத்தமும் சமணமும் பழைய இந்தியாவின் ஷ்ரமண மரபுகளில் வளர்ந்தன. இரண்டும் ஒழுக்கம் மற்றும் விடுதலைப் பாதையை வலியுறுத்தினாலும் அவற்றின் தத்துவக் கருத்துகள் வேறுபட்டவை.

chapters.subject: Geography
chapters.title: Indian Monsoon: Basic Mechanism
chapters.summary: The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds shaped by land-sea heating contrasts and several atmospheric and oceanic factors.

sections.heading: Seasonal pattern
body: The southwest monsoon normally advances over Kerala around the beginning of June, but onset and progress vary from year to year.
The retreating or northeast monsoon is especially important for rainfall over parts of southeastern India, including Tamil Nadu, during October–December.

sections.heading: Why it occurs
bullets: Land heats and cools faster than the ocean, creating seasonal pressure differences.
The northward shift of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone influences the monsoon circulation.
The Himalayas, Tibetan Plateau, cross-equatorial flow and low-pressure systems affect its distribution.
ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole can influence monsoon variability, but neither alone determines every year's rainfall.

sections.heading: Spatial variation
body: The Western Ghats receive heavy orographic rainfall on their windward side, while some interior areas lie in a rain-shadow region.
The northeast monsoon contributes significantly to rainfall in Tamil Nadu and adjoining southeast coastal areas.

prelims: Southwest monsoon is the main rainy season for much of India.
Tamil Nadu receives a substantial share of its rainfall during the northeast/retreating monsoon season.
Orographic rainfall occurs when moist air is forced to rise over relief.
mains: Explain the factors controlling the onset, distribution and variability of the Indian monsoon.
Discuss the importance of the northeast monsoon for Tamil Nadu and water security.

recall.q: Which monsoon season is especially important for Tamil Nadu?
recall.a: The northeast or retreating monsoon, broadly during October–December.

recall.q: What is orographic rainfall?
recall.a: Rainfall caused when moist air rises over a mountain barrier, cools and condenses.

chapters.tamil: இந்திய மழைக்காலம் நிலம்–கடல் வெப்ப வேறுபாடு, காற்றழுத்த அமைப்பு மற்றும் கடல்–வளிமண்டல காரணிகளால் பாதிக்கப்படுகிறது. தமிழ்நாட்டிற்கு வடகிழக்கு பருவமழை மிகவும் முக்கியமானது.

chapters.subject: Geography
chapters.title: Indian River Systems: Himalayan and Peninsular
chapters.summary: India's rivers are commonly studied under Himalayan and Peninsular systems, which differ in origin, flow regime and basin characteristics.

sections.heading: Himalayan rivers
body: Major systems include the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra. Many tributaries are fed by glaciers, snowmelt and rainfall.
They generally have large drainage basins and, in many stretches, flow throughout the year, though discharge varies seasonally.

sections.heading: Peninsular rivers
body: Major east-flowing rivers include the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri; many drain into the Bay of Bengal.
The Narmada and Tapi are major west-flowing rivers that drain into the Arabian Sea. Many Peninsular rivers depend strongly on monsoon rainfall.

sections.heading: Why river basins matter
bullets: River basins support irrigation, drinking water, hydropower, ecosystems and transport.
Inter-state sharing, pollution, floods, droughts and sediment management create governance challenges.
A river basin approach considers upstream and downstream connections rather than administrative boundaries alone.

prelims: Godavari is the largest Peninsular river basin by area.
Narmada and Tapi flow westwards through rift valleys.
Kaveri is an important east-flowing Peninsular river.
mains: Compare Himalayan and Peninsular river systems in terms of origin and flow regime.
Discuss integrated river-basin management and inter-state water cooperation.

recall.q: Name two major west-flowing Peninsular rivers.
recall.a: Narmada and Tapi.

recall.q: Which is the largest Peninsular river basin by area?
recall.a: Godavari.

chapters.tamil: இமயமலை ஆறுகள் பனி உருகுதல் மற்றும் மழையால் ஊட்டம் பெறுகின்றன. தீபகற்ப ஆறுகள் பெரும்பாலும் பருவமழையைச் சார்ந்தவை; கோதாவரி மிகப்பெரிய தீபகற்ப ஆற்றுப் பள்ளத்தாக்காகும்.

chapters.subject: Economy
chapters.title: GDP and National Income: First Concepts
chapters.summary: GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced within a country's domestic territory during a given period.

sections.heading: What GDP measures
body: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is a measure of production within domestic territory over a specified period, usually a quarter or a year.
Only final goods and services are counted to avoid double counting intermediate inputs. GDP can be estimated through production, income and expenditure approaches.

sections.heading: Nominal and real GDP
bullets: Nominal GDP uses current prices and can rise because of higher output, higher prices or both.
Real GDP adjusts for price changes to better track changes in the volume of production.
Per capita GDP is GDP divided by population; it is an average and does not show how income is distributed.

sections.heading: Limits of GDP
body: GDP does not directly measure inequality, unpaid household work, environmental quality, leisure or every dimension of well-being.
Use GDP alongside employment, health, education, poverty and environmental indicators for a broader assessment.

prelims: GDP refers to production within domestic territory.
Real GDP adjusts for price changes; nominal GDP uses current prices.
GDP per capita is an average and does not reveal income distribution.
mains: Explain why GDP growth is important but insufficient as a measure of inclusive development.
Discuss complementary indicators needed to assess human well-being.

recall.q: What is the key difference between nominal and real GDP?
recall.a: Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP adjusts for price changes.

recall.q: Does per capita GDP show how income is distributed?
recall.a: No. It is an average and can conceal inequality.

chapters.tamil: GDP என்பது ஒரு நாட்டின் உள்நாட்டு எல்லைக்குள் ஒரு குறிப்பிட்ட காலத்தில் உற்பத்தி செய்யப்பட்ட இறுதி பொருட்கள் மற்றும் சேவைகளின் மதிப்பு. GDP மட்டும் மக்களின் நலனை முழுமையாகக் காட்டாது.

chapters.subject: Economy
chapters.title: Inflation: Meaning, Causes and Effects
chapters.summary: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, reducing the purchasing power of money.

sections.heading: Meaning and measurement
body: Inflation is a rise in the general price level over time; a rise in one product's price alone is not necessarily inflation.
In India, Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a key measure used for retail inflation. Wholesale Price Index (WPI) tracks price changes at the wholesale level for its basket.

sections.heading: Common causes
bullets: Demand-pull: aggregate demand grows faster than the economy's capacity to supply.
Cost-push: input costs such as fuel, transport or raw materials rise.
Supply shocks: weather events or disruptions reduce availability of essential goods.
Expectations and currency movements can also influence prices.

sections.heading: Effects and policy response
body: High and volatile inflation can reduce purchasing power, create uncertainty and affect households differently.
Monetary policy, supply-side steps, logistics improvements and targeted support can all matter; the suitable response depends on the source of inflation.

prelims: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level.
CPI is a key measure of retail inflation in India.
Demand-pull and cost-push are common analytical categories.
mains: Analyse how inflation affects households with different income levels.
Evaluate the roles of monetary policy and supply-side measures in managing inflation.

recall.q: Does a rise in the price of only one commodity always mean inflation?
recall.a: No. Inflation refers to a sustained rise in the general price level.

recall.q: What does CPI broadly track?
recall.a: Changes in the prices paid by consumers for a representative basket of goods and services.

chapters.tamil: பணவீக்கம் என்பது பொதுவான விலை நிலை தொடர்ந்து உயர்வதாகும். இதனால் பணத்தின் வாங்கும் திறன் குறைகிறது; CPI சில்லறை விலை மாற்றத்தை அளவிடும் முக்கியக் குறியீடு.
